title: Waffle chart for time evolution
text:
NoteCredit



This reproduces a visualization created by Muhammad Azhar for the #30DayChartChallenge, as featured on the R Graph Gallery. Data: NOAA (the storms dataset bundled with the tidyverse). All credit for the original design goes to the author.
A waffle chart showing how the yearly count of Atlantic tropical cyclones, split by storm category, has evolved since 2010.
Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(showtext)
library(ggtext)
library(waffle)
library(MetBrewer)

# Load fonts
font_add_google("Outfit", "title_font")
font_add_google("Cabin", "body_font")
showtext_auto()
title_font <- "title_font"
body_font <- "body_font"

# Prepare data
storms_df <- storms |>
  filter(year >= 2010,
         status %in% c("hurricane", "tropical depression",
                       "tropical storm","tropical wave")) |>
  count(year, status)

# Define text labels
title_text <- "In the Atlantic Ocean, tropical storms are more common than other cyclones."
subtitle_text <- "Tropical Storm is a cyclone with maximum sustained winds of 39 to 73 mph (34 to 63 knots).\nshowing number of cyclones for each year since 2010"
caption_text <- "Graphic: Muhammad Azhar | #30DayChartChallenge | Data: NOAA"

# Create waffle chart
ggplot(storms_df, aes(fill = status, values = n)) +
  geom_waffle(color = "white", size = .25, n_rows = 10, flip = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 1, strip.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_discrete() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) x * 10,
                     expand = c(0,0)) +
  MetBrewer::scale_fill_met_d("Hiroshige", direction=1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = title_text,
       subtitle = subtitle_text,
       caption = caption_text) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(family = body_font, size=12),
    axis.text.y = element_text(family = body_font, size=12),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.spacing = unit(0.5, 'cm'),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.5, 'cm'),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.7, 'cm'),
    legend.text = element_text(family = body_font, size=13, face = 'plain', color = "grey10"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_textbox(margin = margin(20, 0, 10, 0), size = 30,
                                 family = title_font, face = "bold", width = unit(55, "lines")),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(margin = margin(10, 0, 20, 0), size = 16,
                                 family = body_font, color = "grey15"),
    plot.caption = element_text(family=body_font, face="plain", size=14,
                                color="grey40", hjust=.5, margin=margin(20,0,0,0)),
    plot.background = element_rect(color="white", fill="white"),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 40, 20, 40)
  )

title: Waffle chart for time evolution
section: How it is built, step by step
text:
How it is built, step by step
Each tab adds one layer of the recipe on top of the previous one, so you can see what every piece of the final chart contributes. The code for each step is shown below its plot.

1. Counting storms2. Squares3. One block per year4. Square squares5. Colour6. Text7. Theme


The data work is a single count(): one row per year and storm status, which is all geom_waffle() needs. Every square in the finished chart stands for one cyclone.


# A tibble: 8 × 3
   year status                  n
  <dbl> <fct>               <int>
1  2010 hurricane             163
2  2010 tropical depression    72
3  2010 tropical storm        212
4  2011 hurricane             106
5  2011 tropical depression    47
6  2011 tropical storm        256
7  2011 tropical wave           7
8  2012 hurricane             122



head(storms_df, 8)



waffle::geom_waffle() turns those counts into squares. Without faceting all years are pooled into one block, stacked ten squares high.










w2 <- ggplot(storms_df, aes(fill = status, values = n)) +
  geom_waffle(color = "white", size = .25, n_rows = 10, flip = TRUE)
w2



facet_wrap() with nrow = 1 splits the squares into a column per year and moves the year labels to the bottom, which is what makes the chart read as a time series.










w3 <- w2 +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 1, strip.position = "bottom") +
  scale_x_discrete()
w3



coord_equal() keeps the tiles from stretching, and the y-axis labels are multiplied by ten so the axis counts storms rather than rows of squares.










w4 <- w3 +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) x * 10, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_equal()
w4



The four storm categories are coloured with the Hiroshige palette from MetBrewer.










w5 <- w4 +
  MetBrewer::scale_fill_met_d("Hiroshige", direction = 1)
w5



The title states the finding outright rather than describing the chart, with the definition of a tropical storm carried in the subtitle.










w6 <- w5 +
  labs(title = title_text,
       subtitle = subtitle_text,
       caption = caption_text)
w6



The last step does the most visible work: Outfit and Cabin from Google Fonts, no axis titles, the legend moved to the top with squarish keys, and a white background with generous margins.










w6 +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(family = body_font, size = 12),
    axis.text.y = element_text(family = body_font, size = 12),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.spacing = unit(0.5, 'cm'),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.5, 'cm'),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.7, 'cm'),
    legend.text = element_text(family = body_font, size = 13, face = 'plain', color = "grey10"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_textbox(margin = margin(20, 0, 10, 0), size = 30,
                                 family = title_font, face = "bold", width = unit(55, "lines")),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(margin = margin(10, 0, 20, 0), size = 16,
                                 family = body_font, color = "grey15"),
    plot.caption = element_text(family = body_font, face = "plain", size = 14,
                                color = "grey40", hjust = .5, margin = margin(20, 0, 0, 0)),
    plot.background = element_rect(color = "white", fill = "white"),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 40, 20, 40)
  )

title: Ridgeline plot with inside plot and annotations
text:
NoteCredit



This reproduces a visualization created by Ansgar Wolsing for TidyTuesday, as featured on the R Graph Gallery. Data: Kate Pennington (2018), Bay Area Craigslist Rental Housing Posts, 2000-2018. All credit for the original design goes to the author.
A distribution-per-adjective ridgeline of San Francisco Bay Area Craigslist rental prices, with an annotated “legend” plot embedded inside the panel.
Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggtext)
library(ggdist)
library(glue)
library(patchwork)
library(MetBrewer)
library(showtext)

# Fira Sans is not a system font here; pull it from Google via showtext.
font_add_google("Fira Sans", "Fira Sans")
font_add_google("Fira Sans", "Fira Sans SemiBold")
showtext_auto()
# Load datasets (slimmed copies of the originals)
df_plot <- read_csv(file.path("ridgeline-data", "df_plot.csv"))
rent_title_words <- read_csv(file.path("ridgeline-data", "rent_legend.csv"))
rent_stats <- read_csv(file.path("ridgeline-data", "rent_stats.csv"))

# Prepare data
df_plot <- df_plot %>% arrange(desc(mean_price))
df_plot$word <- factor(df_plot$word, levels = unique(df_plot$word))

# Statistics (precomputed from the full rent dataset)
mean_price <- rent_stats$mean_price
median_price <- rent_stats$median_price
n_rental_posts <- rent_stats$n_rental_posts

bg_color <- "grey97"
font_family <- "Fira Sans"

plot_subtitle = glue("Adjectives used to describe houses and apartments
in the San Francisco Bay Area in the titles of rental posts on Craigslist and
how they are related to rental prices. Titles from
{scales::number(n_rental_posts, big.mark = ',')} rental posts on Craigslist
between 2000 and 2018.
The 15 most frequent adjectives are shown.
")

# Main plot
p <- df_plot %>%
  ggplot(aes(word, price)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill_type = "segments", alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_interval() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = median) +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 0, label = "(\U00F8 bedrooms)",
           family = "Fira Sans", size = 3, hjust = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(y = beds),
    geom = "text",
    fun.data = function(x) {
      data.frame(
        y = 0,
        label = sprintf("(%s)", scales::number(mean(ifelse(x > 0, x, NA), na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.1)))},
    family = font_family, size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median_price, col = "grey30", lty = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = median_price + 50, label = "Median rent",
           family = "Fira Sans", size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = toupper) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2500, 20000, 2500)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("VanGogh3")) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 10000), clip = "off") +
  guides(col = "none") +
  labs(
    title = toupper("Nice and Clean - Relatively Low Rent?"),
    subtitle = plot_subtitle,
    caption = "Axis capped at 10,000 USD.<br>
    Data: Pennington, Kate (2018).
    Bay Area Craigslist Rental Housing Posts, 2000-2018.<br>
    Retrieved from github.com/katepennington/historic_bay_area_craigslist_housing_posts/blob/master/clean_2000_2018.csv.zip.
    <br>
    Visualization: Ansgar Wolsing",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rent in USD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = font_family) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = bg_color),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.1, color = "grey75"),
    plot.title = element_text(family = "Fira Sans SemiBold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(
      margin = margin(t = 4, b = 16), size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_textbox_simple(
      margin = margin(t = 12), size = 7
    ),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0, margin = margin(r = -10), family = "Fira Sans SemiBold"),
    plot.margin = margin(4, 4, 4, 4)
  )

# Create legend (inside plot)
df_for_legend <- rent_title_words %>%
  filter(word == "beautiful")

p_legend <- df_for_legend %>%
  ggplot(aes(word, price)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill_type = "segments", alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_interval() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = median) +
  annotate(
    "richtext",
    x = c(0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 1.4, 1.8),
    y = c(1000, 5000, 3000, 2400, 4000),
    label = c("50 % of prices<br>fall within this range", "95 % of prices",
              "80 % of prices", "Median", "Distribution<br>of prices"),
    fill = NA, label.size = 0, family = font_family, size = 2, vjust = 1,
  ) +
  geom_curve(
    data = data.frame(
      x = c(0.7, 0.80, 0.80, 1.225, 1.8),
      xend = c(0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 1.075, 1.8),
      y = c(1800, 5000, 3000, 2300, 3800),
      yend = c(1800, 5000, 3000, 2100, 2500)),
    aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = yend),
    stat = "unique", curvature = 0.2, size = 0.2, color = "grey12",
    arrow = arrow(angle = 20, length = unit(1, "mm"))
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("VanGogh3")) +
  coord_flip(xlim = c(0.75, 1.3), ylim = c(0, 6000), expand = TRUE) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  labs(title = "Legend") +
  theme_void(base_family = font_family) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(family = "Fira Sans SemiBold", size = 9,
                                  hjust = 0.075),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = "grey30", size = 0.2, fill = bg_color))

# Combine main plot with embedded legend
p + inset_element(p_legend, l = 0.6, r = 1.0, t = 0.99, b = 0.7, clip = FALSE)

title: Ridgeline plot with inside plot and annotations
section: How it is built, step by step
text:
How it is built, step by step
Each tab adds one layer of the recipe on top of the previous one, so you can see what every piece of the final chart contributes. The code for each step is shown below its plot.

1. Distributions2. Intervals3. Colour4. Reference line5. Bedroom counts6. Scales and labels7. Theme8. Inset legend9. Combined


ggdist::stat_halfeye() draws a density curve per adjective. coord_flip() is applied from the start so the orientation stays the same across all steps.










step1 <- ggplot(df_plot, aes(word, price)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill_type = "segments", alpha = 0.3) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 10000), clip = "off")
step1



stat_interval() adds the nested 50 / 80 / 95 % interval bars, and stat_summary() marks the median of each group with a point.










step2 <- ggplot(df_plot, aes(word, price)) +
  stat_halfeye(fill_type = "segments", alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_interval() +
  stat_summary(geom = "point", fun = median) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 10000), clip = "off")
step2



The three interval widths get their colours from MetBrewer::met.brewer("VanGogh3"), and the default colour legend is dropped because the inset legend explains it instead.










step3 <- step2 +
  scale_color_manual(values = MetBrewer::met.brewer("VanGogh3")) +
  guides(col = "none")
step3



A dashed geom_hline() at the overall median rent gives every distribution a common anchor to be read against.










step4 <- step3 +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median_price, col = "grey30", lty = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = median_price + 50, label = "Median rent",
           family = font_family, size = 3, hjust = 0)
step4



A text-producing stat_summary() writes the mean number of bedrooms for each adjective at the left edge, which is what keeps the price differences interpretable.










step5 <- step4 +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 0, label = "(\U00F8 bedrooms)",
           family = font_family, size = 3, hjust = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(y = beds),
    geom = "text",
    fun.data = function(x) {
      data.frame(
        y = 0,
        label = sprintf("(%s)", scales::number(mean(ifelse(x > 0, x, NA), na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.1)))},
    family = font_family, size = 2.5
  )
step5



Axis breaks every 2,500 USD, upper-case category labels, and the title, subtitle and caption text.










step6 <- step5 +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = toupper) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(2500, 20000, 2500)) +
  labs(
    title = toupper("Nice and Clean - Relatively Low Rent?"),
    subtitle = plot_subtitle,
    caption = "Axis capped at 10,000 USD.<br>Visualization: Ansgar Wolsing",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Rent in USD"
  )
step6



theme_minimal() plus a light background, vertical-only grid lines, left-aligned category labels and ggtext text boxes that wrap the subtitle and caption.










step7 <- step6 +
  theme_minimal(base_family = font_family) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = bg_color),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.1, color = "grey75"),
    plot.title = element_text(family = "Fira Sans SemiBold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.subtitle = element_textbox_simple(margin = margin(t = 4, b = 16), size = 10),
    plot.caption = element_textbox_simple(margin = margin(t = 12), size = 7),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    axis.text.y = element_text(hjust = 0, margin = margin(r = -10),
                              family = "Fira Sans SemiBold"),
    plot.margin = margin(4, 4, 4, 4)
  )
step7



The annotated legend is a second, standalone plot built from a single adjective (beautiful) with annotate("richtext", ...) labels and geom_curve() arrows.










p_legend



patchwork::inset_element() places the legend in the empty space at the top right of the main panel.










step7 + inset_element(p_legend, l = 0.6, r = 1.0, t = 0.99, b = 0.7, clip = FALSE)

title: Brussels health-precarity map
text:
NoteCredit



This recreates the building-level map from Bruxelles malade, a data-journalism investigation by the Belgian cooperative magazine Médor. The original is a scroll-driven D3/Mapbox map; here it is rebuilt in R from the same underlying data (the article’s own building-footprint and per-sector data files). All credit for the reporting and design goes to Médor.
The original shades Brussels’ building footprints by a health-precarity index (dim) on a dark basemap. Since the piece is not written in R, I extracted its merged-buildings geometry (721 dissolved footprints, one per statistical sector, each carrying its dim value) and rebuilt the map with sf and ggplot2, reusing Médor’s exact color ramp. Higher values (red) mean more precarious; lower values (teal) mean better off. Hover over a district to highlight it and see its area-weighted average index (rendered interactively with ggiraph).
The pattern is the article’s central finding: a “poor croissant” of high-index (red) neighbourhoods curls through the inner-city and industrial west (Molenbeek, Anderlecht, Saint-Josse), while the wealthier south-east (Uccle, Woluwe) sits at the teal end. The extracted per-sector data also carries the other indicators used in the piece (air pollution no2/pm25, green coverage, noise, diabetes rates, cancer-screening uptake), so the same footprints can be recolored by any of them.
Show code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(ggiraph)
crs_local <- 3812 # Belgian Lambert 2008

# Building footprints, each carrying the precarity index `dim`
buildings <- read_sf(file.path("choropleth-data", "bxlBuildings.topo.json")) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |>
  st_transform(crs_local) |>
  # the sector code's first 5 digits are the commune (NIS) code
  mutate(commune_code = substr(sector, 1, 5),
         area = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)))

# Commune outlines + labels, dissolved from the statistical sectors
sectors <- read_sf(file.path("choropleth-data", "brusselsSectors.json")) |>
  st_set_crs(4326) |>
  st_transform(crs_local) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  mutate(commune_code = substr(cd_sector, 1, 5))

communes <- sectors |>
  group_by(commune_code, commune = tx_munty_descr_fr) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop")

# Area-weighted average index per district (commune)
district_dim <- buildings |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(dim)) |>
  group_by(commune_code) |>
  summarise(dim_district = weighted.mean(dim, area), .groups = "drop")

communes <- communes |>
  left_join(district_dim, by = "commune_code") |>
  mutate(tooltip = sprintf("%s\nPrecarity index: %.1f", commune, dim_district),
         label_pt = st_point_on_surface(geometry))

# Médor's diverging ramp with the article's exact break points (dim 0 -> 50)
stops <- c(0, 11, 14, 18, 24, 29, 34, 41, 50)
cols  <- c("#00939C", "#49A6AE", "#65B3BA", "#B2DCDF", "#FEEEE8",
           "#F8C0AA", "#EC9370", "#DA6436", "#C22E00")

bg <- "#1b1b1b"

p <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings, aes(fill = dim), color = NA) +
  # interactive district layer: transparent until hovered
  geom_sf_interactive(
    data = communes,
    aes(tooltip = tooltip, data_id = commune_code),
    fill = "transparent", color = "white", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_sf_text(data = communes, aes(label = commune, geometry = label_pt),
               color = "grey85", size = 2.6, fontface = "bold", check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = cols,
    values = rescale(stops, from = c(0, 50)),
    limits = c(0, 50), oob = squish,
    na.value = "#3a3a3a",
    name = "Health-precarity index",
    guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = unit(45, "mm"), barheight = unit(4, "mm"),
                            title.position = "top", ticks = FALSE)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "A divided city",
    subtitle = "Building footprints shaded by Médor's index — hover a district for its average",
    caption = "Data extracted from Médor, 'Bruxelles malade'."
  ) +
  coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = bg, color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = bg, color = NA),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    legend.title = element_text(color = "grey85", size = 9),
    legend.text = element_text(color = "grey85", size = 8),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "white", margin = margin(b = 2)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey70", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey55", size = 8, hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 8)),
    plot.margin = margin(12, 12, 12, 12)
  )

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8.5, height_svg = 9,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill:#ffffff55;stroke:white;stroke-width:1.5px;"),
    opts_tooltip(css = "background:#1b1b1b;color:white;padding:6px 10px;border-radius:4px;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:12px;white-space:pre;"),
    opts_toolbar(saveaspng = FALSE),
    opts_sizing(rescale = TRUE)
  )
)

title: Brussels health-precarity map
section: How it is built, step by step
text:
How it is built, step by step
Each tab adds one layer of the recipe on top of the previous one, so you can see what every piece of the final map contributes. The code for each step is shown below its plot.

1. The geometry2. Footprints3. Médor’s colour ramp4. District outlines5. Dark theme6. Interactivity


The extracted footprints are one dissolved polygon per statistical sector, each carrying its precarity index. Reprojecting to Belgian Lambert 2008 (EPSG:3812) is what lets areas be measured in metres for the weighted averages later.


Simple feature collection with 5 features and 4 fields
Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 649160.6 ymin: 662037.4 xmax: 653864.1 ymax: 676549.2
Projected CRS: ETRS89 / Belgian Lambert 2008
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  sector    commune_code   dim    area                                  geometry
  <chr>     <chr>        <dbl>   <dbl>                        <MULTIPOLYGON [m]>
1 21016A214 21016         16.6  13468. (((650239.5 665856.3, 650264.4 665862.1,…
2 21005A322 21005         81.4   1600. (((651418.2 668120.7, 651456 668075.6, 6…
3 21015A33- 21015         36.3  42855. (((650841.3 671842.5, 650818.3 671832.1,…
4 21016A342 21016          4.1 207838. (((650972.6 662044.7, 650958.4 662037.4,…
5 21004G30- 21004         25.3  83727. (((653228.5 675861.2, 653216 675867.3, 6…



buildings |>
  select(sector, commune_code, dim, area) |>
  head(5)



A single geom_sf() with no outline colour. At this zoom the footprints read as texture rather than individual buildings, which is the effect the original is after.










m2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = buildings, aes(fill = dim), color = NA)
m2



The default blue gradient hides the story. scale_fill_gradientn() with the article’s nine stops and colours puts the neutral cream tone at the middle of the index, so teal and red read as “better off” and “more precarious”.










m3 <- m2 +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = cols,
    values = rescale(stops, from = c(0, 50)),
    limits = c(0, 50), oob = squish,
    na.value = "#3a3a3a",
    name = "Health-precarity index",
    guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = unit(45, "mm"), barheight = unit(4, "mm"),
                            title.position = "top", ticks = FALSE)
  )
m3



The commune boundaries and their names give the reader somewhere to stand. The outline layer is geom_sf_interactive() with a transparent fill: it is invisible until hovered, when it becomes the highlight and tooltip target.










m4 <- m3 +
  geom_sf_interactive(
    data = communes,
    aes(tooltip = tooltip, data_id = commune_code),
    fill = "transparent", color = "white", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_sf_text(data = communes, aes(label = commune, geometry = label_pt),
               color = "grey85", size = 2.6, fontface = "bold", check_overlap = TRUE)
m4



theme_void() strips the axes and graticule, and the near-black background is what makes the ramp glow the way the original does. The legend sits top-left, above the map.

title: Multiple Sequence Alignments with r-gt!
text:
NoteCredit



This page reproduces work created by Victor Yuan for the 2025 Posit Table Contest: Visualizing Conserved Regions Across Coronavirus Spike Proteins (contest entry · source code). All credit for the original analysis and design goes to the author.
Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) is a computational technique to compare biological sequences, and identify regions of similarity and differences. This approach is used for identifying conserved functional domains, and understanding evolutionary relationships between related proteins.
For the 2025 Posit Table contest I wanted to explore how MSAs can be effectively visualized using the r package gt. This has been something I have wanted to do for a long time, and I’m excited to share this exploration.
The data we are working with is an MSA from (Wang et al. 2021), where they identified a potential universally conserved “weak spot” in Coronavirus spike proteins to specific cross-reactive monoclonal antibodies. The spike protein was the primary target for developing the COVID-19 vaccines, which crucially saved millions of lives during in the fight against the pandemic.
Figure 5 from their study presents an MSA comparing spike proteins from several coronavirus species: SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and HCoV-OC43 (which causes the common cold). This visualization left an immediate impression on me. Despite there being large divergence between these species, the authors were able to identify a region with enough similarity to serve as target for broadly reactive antibodies.
Let’s explore how we can leverage gt to better understand the evolutionary relationships between coronavirus protein sequences!

library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)

here <- function(...) file.path("data", ...)

# Buenos Aires subway lines and their official colors
line_colors <- c(
  A = "#18cccc", B = "#eb0909", C = "#233aa8",
  D = "#02db2e", E = "#c618cc", H = "#ffdd00"
)

# --- Real geography -------------------------------------------------------
map_caba <- st_read(here("barrios.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)

stations <- readr::read_csv(here("stations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(line = linea, station = estacion) |>
  filter(line %in% names(line_colors))

set.seed(42)

# --- Placeholder passenger data -------------------------------------------
# Per-station total passengers for the month
stations <- stations |>
  mutate(pax_station = round(runif(n(), 5e4, 6e5)))

# Hourly distribution per line (a plausible double-peaked commuter shape)
base_hour <- dnorm(0:23, 8, 2) + 0.8 * dnorm(0:23, 18, 2.5) + 0.05
hourly <- map_dfr(names(line_colors), function(ln) {
  w <- base_hour * runif(24, 0.7, 1.3)
  tibble(line = ln, hour = 0:23, pax_total = round(w / sum(w) * 4e6))
})

# Daily evolution per line across the month
daily <- map_dfr(names(line_colors), function(ln) {
  d <- seq(as.Date("2021-11-01"), as.Date("2021-11-30"), by = "day")
  wk <- ifelse(format(d, "%u") %in% c("6", "7"), 0.45, 1)
  tibble(line = ln, date = d,
         pax_total = round(wk * runif(length(d), 8e4, 1.3e5)))
})

# Circular mean hour, weighted by passengers (replaces the {circular} pkg)
mean_hours <- hourly |>
  group_by(line) |>
  summarise(
    mean_hour = {
      ang <- hour / 24 * 2 * pi
      m <- atan2(sum(pax_total * sin(ang)), sum(pax_total * cos(ang)))
      (m / (2 * pi) * 24) %% 24
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# --- Plot builders (ported from the original R code) ----------------------
fig_clock_plot <- function(.line) {
  mean_hour <- mean_hours$mean_hour[mean_hours$line == .line]
  temp <- hourly |>
    filter(line == .line) |>
    mutate(color_hour = hour == round(mean_hour))
  ggplot(temp, aes(hour, pax_total)) +
    geom_col(color = "white", fill = "lightgrey") +
    coord_polar(start = 0) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = mean_hour, color = line_colors[[.line]], linewidth = 2) +
    geom_label(
      aes(y = max(pax_total) + quantile(pax_total, 0.3),
          color = color_hour, label = hour),
      size = 6, label.size = NA, show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("black", line_colors[[.line]])) +
    scale_x_continuous("", limits = c(0, 24), breaks = 0:24) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::unit_format(unit = "K", scale = 1e-3)) +
    labs(y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 22, color = "grey"),
          axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
}

fig_map <- function(.line) {
  temp <- stations |>
    filter(line == .line) |>
    mutate(pax_percent = pax_station / sum(pax_station))
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = map_caba, color = "black", fill = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_point(
      data = temp, aes(long, lat, size = pax_percent),
      alpha = 0.7, fill = line_colors[[.line]], color = "black", shape = 21
    ) +
    scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 9), guide = "none") +
    theme_void()
}

fig_evol <- function(.line) {
  ggplot(filter(daily, line == .line), aes(date, pax_total)) +
    geom_line(color = "grey", linewidth = 2.5) +
    geom_line(color = line_colors[[.line]], linewidth = 1.5) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::unit_format(unit = "K", scale = 1e-3)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(text = element_text(size = 22),
          panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
}

# --- One row per line -----------------------------------------------------
tbl_data <- stations |>
  group_by(line) |>
  summarise(
    most_used_station = station[which.max(pax_station)],
    pax_total = sum(pax_station),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    variation = runif(n(), -0.12, 0.18),
    route = c(
      "Plaza de Mayo - San Pedrito", "Alem - J. M. de Rosas",
      "Retiro - Constitución", "Catedral - Congreso de Tucumán",
      "Bolívar - Plaza de los Virreyes", "Facultad de Derecho - Hospitales"

  rowwise() |>
  mutate(passengers_type = list(as.numeric(round(prop.table(runif(3)) * 100)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(line, route, most_used_station, clock_plot, pax_total, variation,

evol_plots   <- map(tbl_data$line, fig_evol)
